title: There Are Two Types of Cannabis Black Markets: One Problematic, One Benign

content_html_sanitized:
First, on the subject of black markets, I have to discuss something so absurd that it could cause brain damage, so please put on your tinfoil hat.

 

Kyle Jaeger reported on the excellent website, Marijuana Moment that a member of Congress actually argued that legalizing cannabis would help Chinese organized crime, and putting it back in the black market would hurt them!

 

So… did the mafia take over the alcohol business after alcohol prohibition was repealed? And if you were in the petunia business, would you rather compete with someone who has guns and pays no taxes and has employees who ignore the law, or a legitimate business owner who is subject to the law?

 

I defy them to find one business professor anywhere who agrees with that.

 

By the very nature of black markets it is impossible to know how big they really are, but there are estimates that as much as 75% of the current US cannabis supply is still in the black market. There are similar estimates for the Canadian market.

 

There are two reasons for the persistence of the black markets, one problematic and one benign.

 

The benign contraband market is the traditional artisanal market consisting of growers who love the plant and who have developed a customer base over the years. These people have nothing to do with organized crime, whether Chinese or whatever. They are benefiting the community.

See

The Decline and Fall of Humboldt County

 

The more problematic market is more likely to still be “Mexican”, for obvious historical and geographical reasons. This market is thriving because “legalization” involves so many taxes and regulations that these growers can easily undercut the legal market on price, and even on convenience when there are no legal retailers in large rural areas. There may also be cultural barriers in minority neighborhoods. The gentry goes to “dispensaries”. The workers go to the corner.

 

Then there are all the other regulations. Minorities were disproportionately targeted by the police under prohibition, so minority politicians get to pick a few well connected members of their community to get licenses to compensate for the collective injustice.

 

Of course, that raises prices and limits the number of outlets. So, minority cannabis users end up paying more and having less selection to compensate the friends of the politicians. The contraband dealers, who may also sell hard drugs also benefit.

 

The cornerstone or bodega can sell beer and cigarettes, but they can’t sell a small quantity of cannabis. There are actually far to few cannabis retailers. Protecting the public? Think of the children!

 

In New York the laws authorizing retail outlets required that they be at least 500 feet from schools and 200 feet from churches or other houses of worship.

 

Frankly, I find the latter outrageous, and the former counterproductive. Kids are much less likely to go into a store across the street from their school where they would be visible. And shouldn’t churches want sinners to get as close as possible to God?

 

Meanwhile, at least 47 cannabis dispensaries opened too close to schools after an attorney questioned regulators’ buffer zone measurement method. Of course, the state wanted the stores to move because of its mistakes. (It caved.)

 

And then there are perfectly reasonable sounding regulations for “product safety.” Of course, I can go to a Farmers Market and buy something to eat from someone I trust, but I can’t buy something to smoke.

 

In fact, the only widespread poisoning from marijuana that has been reported was actually done by the United States government.

See Poisoning the People

 

The cannabis industry has lost billions of dollars and the black market still dominates the supply, not because there has been too little regulation, but because there has been too much.

 

As for taxation, taxes should be set to be competitive with the black markets. In any case, the best way to maximize the economic benefits (and taxes) of the legal cannabis market is to maximize employment. Cannabis social clubs and Farmers Markets should be encouraged.

 

Freedom should be encouraged.
